column2: An offeree replying that the offered goods will be bought only at a lower price ordinarily makes a counteroffer rather than absolute unqualified acceptance of the original price.
column3: That conditional lower-price response concludes the original contract at the original offered price because it communicates interest in buying.

column2: Indian law can recognise consideration moving from another person, while the general rule on a stranger enforcing a contract remains distinct and subject to recognised exceptions.
column3: Because consideration can move from another person, every nonparty providing it acquires an unrestricted right to sue on the contract.

column2: A past act done at the promisor's desire can qualify as consideration under Indian law; it is distinguished from treating every unsolicited past favour as automatic consideration.
column3: Only future acts can qualify as consideration under Indian law even when the past act was expressly done at the promisor's desire.

column2: A minor's generally void agreement is distinguished from a qualifying claim for necessaries reimbursable from the minor's property rather than ordinary personal contractual liability.
column3: Supplying qualifying necessaries validates the minor's entire borrowing agreement and creates the same personal liability as an adult's contract.

column2: A person usually of unsound mind may contract during an interval when able to understand and form rational judgment about the contract's effect, subject to other capacity conditions.
column3: A history of unsoundness makes every lucid-interval contract void regardless of actual competence when contracting.

column2: Mere silence is not invariably fraud; a duty to speak or circumstances making silence equivalent to speech can change the statutory analysis.
column3: Silence can never constitute fraud because no express spoken or written statement was made.

column2: Both parties mistaken about an essential existing fact can make an agreement void; a mistake only about the goods' market value is not automatically the same essential-fact mistake.
column3: Every shared mistaken estimate of market value automatically voids the agreement as an essential-fact mistake.

column2: A qualifying coercion-induced contract is generally voidable at the affected party's option, distinct from an agreement void from inception for an unlawful object.
column3: Both a qualifying coercion-induced contract and an unlawful-object agreement are automatically enforceable at the wrongdoer's sole option.

column2: Inadequate consideration alone does not necessarily make an agreement void, while it can be relevant evidence when examining whether consent was freely given.
column3: Any difference between consideration and market value automatically makes the agreement void without considering consent or other statutory rules.

column2: The general Indian statutory rule on restraint of trade must be read with its recognised exceptions, including a qualifying restraint connected with sale of goodwill.
column3: A commercially reasonable label validates every restraint of trade without considering the statutory rule or recognised exceptions.

column2: An obligation contingent on a collateral uncertain event follows the relevant event rules; an unconditional obligation does not become contingent merely because performing it may be difficult.
column3: Any uncertainty about the promisor's ability to perform converts an unconditional contract into a contingent contract.

column2: A rise in performance cost or reduction in expected profit does not by itself establish supervening legal impossibility or frustration.
column3: A contract is automatically frustrated once the promisor's expected profit becomes negative.

column2: Agreed substitution of a new contract is novation; the promisee's remission of performance under the statutory rule is a distinct discharge mechanism.
column3: A promisee accepting less under the remission rule necessarily creates a three-party novation in every case.

column2: Loss naturally arising from breach and loss within the relevant contemplation rules are distinguished from remote indirect loss; every claimed consequential amount is not automatically recoverable.
column3: Proof that a loss occurred after breach alone establishes full recoverability regardless of foreseeability or remoteness.

column2: A surety's liability is generally co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless the guarantee provides otherwise; the creditor need not first exhaust every remedy against the debtor merely because there is a surety.
column3: The creditor must always exhaust every remedy against the principal debtor before any surety liability can arise.

column2: Delivery of a laptop for repair transfers possession for a purpose with return obligations, rather than ownership as in a sale of that laptop.
column3: Handing the laptop to the repairer transfers ownership because physical possession and legal ownership are identical.

column2: A pledge is bailment of goods as security, creating a security purpose beyond ordinary custody; not every bailment is therefore a pledge.
column3: Every bailment is a pledge because temporary possession always secures repayment of a debt.

column2: A principal's liability analysis can distinguish actual and apparent authority; an agent's undisclosed private instruction does not alone settle what a third party was reasonably led to believe by the principal's conduct.
column3: A private limit unknown to a third party automatically defeats every apparent-authority claim regardless of the principal's own representations.

column2: A breach of condition and a breach of warranty have different ordinary remedy consequences under sale-of-goods rules, with statutory circumstances in which a condition can be treated as a warranty.
column3: Every breached condition necessarily permits rejection even when the applicable statutory circumstances require warranty treatment.

column2: Sale-of-goods risk rules depend on the applicable statutory defaults and agreement; physical possession alone does not determine title and risk in every transaction.
column3: Risk and title always pass together with physical delivery regardless of the agreement and applicable statutory qualifications.

column2: The ordinary rule that a non-owner cannot confer better title is subject to recognised sale-of-goods exceptions; stating the default does not resolve every mercantile-agent or estoppel case.
column3: A buyer can never obtain valid title from a non-owner under any recognised statutory exception.

column2: Lien generally concerns goods still in the seller's possession, whereas stoppage in transit addresses qualifying goods in transit when the buyer is insolvent.
column3: Stoppage in transit requires the seller to retain physical possession, making it identical to an unpaid seller's lien.

column1: Holder versus holder in due course
column2: Holder-in-due-course status requires the relevant consideration, timing and good-faith conditions; ordinary possession alone does not establish those additional protections.
column3: Any possessor of a negotiable instrument is a holder in due course even after acquiring it overdue with notice of a title defect.

column2: A cheque is a bill drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand; a bill payable at a future date is not a cheque merely because a bank processes it.
column3: Every future-dated bill becomes a cheque when presented through a bank for collection.

column2: A company's separate legal personality is distinct from the extent of member liability; recognition of the entity does not mean directors are immune from every personal statutory liability.
column3: Separate personality removes all possible personal statutory liability of directors for their own misconduct.

column2: An LLP partner acts as agent of the LLP for its business rather than automatically as agent of every other partner; fraud and other statutory exceptions require separate analysis.
column3: Every LLP partner is automatically an agent of each other partner with unlimited personal liability for all partnership acts.

column2: Competition-law analysis concerns market conduct and competitive effects under the relevant provisions; a dominant position alone is distinguished from abuse of that position.
column3: Holding a dominant position alone establishes unlawful abuse without examining conduct under the applicable rules.

column2: Legal recognition of electronic records and qualifying electronic signatures does not establish that every scanned signature image meets every statutory authentication requirement.
column3: Any pasted image of a handwritten signature automatically satisfies all statutory digital-signature requirements.

column2: The right to information operates with statutory exemptions and procedures; labelling a document confidential alone does not settle the applicable exemption analysis.
column3: Every document marked confidential is automatically exempt from RTI without examining a statutory ground.

column2: GST treatment requires analysing supply type, place-of-supply and applicable conditions; a firm's GST registration alone does not prove every inward tax amount is creditable.
column3: Every inward tax payment by a registered firm is automatically eligible input tax credit regardless of blocked-credit and use conditions.
